name: Vinaceous-Buff
lede: Vinaceous-Buff is a wine-tinted tan, one of a long family of "vinaceous" names Robert Ridgway coined for naturalists describing birds and mammals with a faint reddish-purple cast.

sections.title: Wine plus tan
sections.body:
Ridgway carried this name over from his own 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, then replated it in 1912 at plate XL, hue 17''', tone d [1]. "Vinaceous" is Ridgway's own coinage, built from *vinaceus*, Latin for wine-colored, and used across dozens of his plates to mark a hue leaning toward wine-red rather than true brown [1]. The ISCC-NBS system later filed it as block 28, a brownish pink [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[sandust]], [[dusty-peach]], [[pastel-parchment]] and [[pale-blush]], at 3.5, 4.4, 4.5 and 4.8 ΔE [1]. Measured in LCH it is lightness 74, chroma 17 and hue 68 degrees, a muted, pale orange-brown [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this tan in 1,487 of 23,781 paintings (6.25%, as photographed), more common than 90% of the named colors we track [3]. It most often plays a hidden color, found this way in 41% of its 1,006 strongest matches [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from Nepal, at 3.8 times the expected rate [3]. Ludolf Bakhuysen is its most devoted painter, at 5.0 times the baseline rate across his 20 works here [3]. The earliest dated match runs to the year 900, nearly a thousand years before Ridgway's 1886 record; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the pigment was there, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature (1912), carried over from 1886
